BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: back pain is one of the commonest presentations in medicine — and hides emergencies (cauda equina, cord compression, infection, malignancy). This subtab ties the spine together into the disc prolapse, radiculopathy, the red flags and lumbar puncture you’ll be examined on and will meet on the wards.
Back Pain & Red Flags
Mechanical (most common)
  • Worse on movement, better with rest; no systemic features; muscular/ligamentous or degenerative (spondylosis)
Red flags → investigate
  • Cauda equina — saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica
  • Malignancy — age >50, weight loss, night pain, past cancer
  • Infection — fever, IVDU, immunosuppression (discitis/epidural abscess)
  • Fracture — trauma, osteoporosis, steroids
  • Inflammatory — young, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise (ankylosing spondylitis)
Intervertebral Disc Prolapse & Radiculopathy
Mechanism
  • The nucleus pulposus herniates through a torn annulus fibrosus, usually posterolaterally (the posterior longitudinal ligament is strong centrally)
  • It compresses the traversing (lower) nerve root — e.g. an L4/5 disc typically hits the L5 root
Common levels
  • L4/5 disc → L5 root: weak big-toe extension (EHL), numb dorsum of foot, walking on heels difficult
  • L5/S1 disc → S1 root: weak plantarflexion, numb sole/lateral foot, reduced ankle jerk
Sciatica is radicular leg pain in a dermatomal pattern; the straight-leg-raise (Lasègue’s) test reproduces it (L5/S1), while the femoral stretch test targets higher roots (L2–L4).
Cauda Equina Syndrome
Why it happens
  • The spinal cord ends at L1/L2 (conus medullaris); below that the cauda equina (lumbosacral roots) floats in CSF
  • A large central disc prolapse (or tumour/abscess) compresses these roots
Red-flag features
  • Saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention (then overflow), faecal incontinence/loss of anal tone
  • Bilateral sciatica & lower-limb weakness (LMN pattern)
Surgical emergency. Suspected cauda equina needs an urgent MRI and decompression — delay risks permanent bladder, bowel & sexual dysfunction.
Cord vs Cauda Equina — Localising the Lesion
FeatureCord (conus/above)Cauda equina
Neuron typeUMN (below the level)LMN
WeaknessSymmetrical, spasticAsymmetrical, flaccid
ReflexesHyperreflexia, up-going plantarsAreflexia, down-going
SensoryA sensory levelSaddle / dermatomal (roots)
SphinctersEarly (conus) — spastic bladderLater — flaccid, retention
Spinal cord compression (e.g. metastasis) is also an emergency: back pain, a sensory level, UMN signs below and bladder involvement → urgent MRI whole spine & steroids.
Vertebral Fractures & Deformity
Fractures
  • Wedge/compression — osteoporotic (elderly, steroids); loss of anterior height
  • Burst — axial load; retropulsion of bone into the canal (can be unstable)
  • Chance — flexion-distraction (“seat-belt”); often with intra-abdominal injury
  • Stability depends on Denis’ three columns (anterior, middle, posterior)
Deformity
  • Kyphosis (excess thoracic flexion), lordosis (lumbar extension), scoliosis (lateral curve + rotation)
  • Spondylolisthesis — a vertebra slips forward on the one below
  • Spondylosis — degenerative disc/facet disease; spinal stenosis → neurogenic claudication
Lumbar Puncture & Spinal/Epidural Anaesthesia
Where & why
  • Performed at L3/L4 or L4/5 — below the conus (L1/2), so the needle meets only cauda equina roots (which move aside)
  • Tuffier’s line (between the iliac crests) marks the L4 spinous process / L3–4 space
Layers pierced (to CSF)
  • Skin → superficial fascia → supraspinous → interspinous → ligamentum flavum → epidural (extradural) space → dura → arachnoid → subarachnoid space (CSF)
  • Spinal anaesthesia = into the CSF (subarachnoid); epidural = into the epidural space (no dural puncture)
Neural Tube Defects
Spina bifida occulta — a failed vertebral arch fusion only (a tuft of hair/dimple); usually asymptomatic.
Meningocele — meninges herniate through the defect (cord normal).
Myelomeningocele — meninges and neural tissue herniate → neurological deficit; associated with Chiari II & hydrocephalus.
Prevention — peri-conceptional folic acid; screened by a raised maternal AFP.
Clinical Signs & Roots
Straight-leg raise (Lasègue) — stretches the sciatic nerve (L5/S1 roots) → reproduces radicular pain.
Femoral stretch test — prone knee flexion → anterior-thigh pain (L2–L4 roots).
Key reflexes — knee jerk L3/4, ankle jerk S1; plantar up-going = UMN.
Dermatome anchors — nipple T4, umbilicus T10, groin L1, knee L3/4, big toe L5, little toe/sole S1.
🧠 Mnemonics
Cauda equina red flags — Saddle anaesthesia, Bladder/Bowel dysfunction, Bilateral sciatica → urgent MRI.
LP level — go below the conus (L1/2): L3/4 or L4/5 (Tuffier’s line = L4).
Disc rule — the disc hits the lower (traversing) root: L4/5 → L5; L5/S1 → S1.
“S1 = ankle jerk; L3/4 = knee jerk.”
⭐ Exam Pearls
Discs prolapse posterolaterally & hit the traversing root: L4/5 → L5, L5/S1 → S1.
Cauda equina = saddle anaesthesia + painless retention + bilateral sciatica → emergency MRI & decompression.
Cord ends at L1/L2 (conus); below is cauda equina — LP is done at L3/4 or L4/5.
Cord lesion = UMN + sensory level; cauda equina = LMN + saddle/root pattern.
Cord compression (mets) = back pain + sensory level + UMN signs → urgent MRI + steroids.
LP layers: supraspinous → interspinous → ligamentum flavum → dura → arachnoid → CSF.
Spinal = subarachnoid (CSF); epidural = epidural space (no dural puncture).
Osteoporotic wedge fractures lose anterior vertebral height; burst fractures can be unstable.
Myelomeningocele = cord + meninges herniate (deficit); prevented by folic acid.
SLR = L5/S1; femoral stretch = L2–L4.
